youtube.baslik: Auditory Rehabilitation for Children with Implants | Lesson 268 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
After cochlear implant activation, how does a child learn to make sense of sound? In this lesson we cover auditory skill goals, family involvement, the CAP, SIR and IT-MAIS scales, the expected developmental path by hearing age and the factors that affect outcomes.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Archbold, Lutman and Marshall, Categories of auditory performance, Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol Suppl (1995); Allen, Nikolopoulos and O'Donoghue, Speech intelligibility in children after cochlear implantation, Am J Otol (1998); Zimmerman-Phillips, Robbins and Osberger, Assessing cochlear implant benefit in very young children, Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol Suppl (2000); Niparko et al., Spoken language development in children following cochlear implantation, JAMA (2010); Estabrooks, MacIver-Lux and Rhoades, Auditory-Verbal Therapy: Science, Research, and Practice.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Goals, family involvement, CAP, SIR and IT-MAIS
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about auditory rehabilitation and auditory skill goals after activation in children with cochlear implants.
We will also cover the auditory performance, speech intelligibility and parent scales that track progress, and the expected path.

maddeler.metin: The implant gives sound, the brain _learns_

cumleler: A cochlear implant delivers sound to the auditory nerve, but the child's brain learns over time to make sense of it.
So if the child had no adequate access with hearing aids, hearing age is counted from implant activation.
Learning requires the processor to be worn every waking hour; data logging shows this objectively.
Mapping and rehabilitation go together; a good map provides audibility, and rehabilitation teaches the use of that sound.
We saw pediatric programming and objective measures in a separate lesson; this lesson focuses on how the sound is used.
The process is teamwork, with the family, the audiologist and the therapist working together.
After activation the child starts to receive sound, for the first time or again; first reactions may be surprise, crying or stillness.
In the first weeks, the goal is awareness of sounds and turning when a sound comes; turning to one's name is a key sign of this stage.
Next, the meaning of environmental sounds such as the doorbell, a dog barking and the phone is learned.
Then differences in duration, rhythm and melody of speech sounds, and later vowels and consonants, begin to be discriminated.
Word meaning is first built with words heard often in daily routines, such as mama, water and come.
The pace of these steps varies greatly; a child with previous hearing experience may move through them faster.
The first goal is for the child to turn to their name from different distances and directions.
Detecting and then identifying the Ling sounds is daily evidence of access to speech frequencies.
Recognizing environmental sounds teaches the child that a sound has a source and a meaning.
In a closed set, the child picks the word heard from a small number of choices; for example, from three pictures.
In an open set, no choices are given; the child repeats or answers what was heard.
Advanced goals are understanding without seeing the speaker's face, in noise, at a distance and on the phone.
The family's first task is to keep the processor on all day; data logging is read together with the family at every visit.
In young children the coil and processor fall off easily; a headband, hair clip and safety cord reduce this problem.
Routines such as bath time, meals, dressing and play are natural chances to practice listening.
A parent narrating what they do, singing and answering the child's vocal attempts enriches the language environment.
Reading books together every day increases vocabulary and listening time.
Meeting families with similar experiences gives the family strength, especially in the first months.
Young children cannot do long speech tests, so progress is tracked with scales.
These scales rely on the parent's daily observations or on the clinician placing the child's skills into set categories.
When the same scale is repeated at regular intervals, the child's own developmental path emerges.
Scales give the audiologist, therapist, surgeon and family a shared language, and make it easier to compare results across centers.
But scales only classify roughly; they do not replace detailed language and speech tests.

cumleler.yazi: The Categories of Auditory Performance, or CAP, were described by Archbold and colleagues in 1995.
cumleler.ses: The Categories of Auditory Performance, or C A P, were described by Archbold and colleagues in nineteen ninety five.

cumleler: The clinician places the child's everyday auditory ability into one of eight categories, from zero to seven.
Zero is no awareness of environmental sounds; one is awareness of environmental sounds; two is responding to speech sounds.
Three is identifying environmental sounds; four is discriminating some speech sounds without speechreading.
Five is understanding common phrases without speechreading; six is understanding conversation with a familiar talker without speechreading.
Seven is using the phone with a familiar talker; a revised version adds two higher categories, such as group conversation in noise.
The steps in the graph show an example child's progress over the years after implantation; the real pace varies from child to child.

cumleler.yazi: The Speech Intelligibility Rating, or SIR, classifies spontaneous speech into five categories.
cumleler.ses: The Speech Intelligibility Rating, or S I R, classifies spontaneous speech into five categories.

cumleler: In category one, connected speech is unintelligible; the child does not yet produce recognizable words and may communicate in other ways.
In category two, connected speech is still unintelligible, but single words begin to be understood with context and speechreading.
In category three, connected speech can be understood by a listener who concentrates and speechreads.
In category four, connected speech is understood by a listener with little experience of the speech of people with hearing loss.

cumleler.yazi: In category five, connected speech is understood by all listeners; CAP and SIR are often reported together.
cumleler.ses: In category five, connected speech is understood by all listeners; C A P and S I R are often reported together.

maddeler.metin: MAIS for older children, LittlEARS for infants

cumleler.yazi: The Infant-Toddler Meaningful Auditory Integration Scale, or IT-MAIS, is a structured interview with the parent.
cumleler.ses: The Infant-Toddler Meaningful Auditory Integration Scale, or I T mays, is a structured interview with the parent.

cumleler: Its ten questions are each scored from 0 to 4, so the total is at most 40.
The questions first ask about the child's vocal behavior and vocal reactions when the processor is put on.
Then they ask whether the child turns to their name and orients to sounds spontaneously at home and in new places.
The last questions are about deriving meaning from sound, for example telling familiar sounds apart.

cumleler.yazi: The MAIS, with the same structure, is used for older children, and the LittlEARS auditory questionnaire is common under age two.
cumleler.ses: The mays, with the same structure, is used for older children, and the little ears auditory questionnaire is common under age two.

cumleler: In a child with an implant, language development is tracked against hearing age rather than chronological age.
The general goal is at least one year of language growth for each year of hearing; the dashed line shows this goal.
Many children implanted early with strong family involvement follow this line, and even catch up with peers over time.

cumleler.yazi: In a multicenter study in the US, children implanted at a younger age showed faster spoken language growth.
cumleler.ses: In a multicenter study in the U S, children implanted at a younger age showed faster spoken language growth.

cumleler: In some children the line is flatter, which may suggest additional needs, low use or a problem with audibility.
The lines in the graph are examples; each child's own line is tracked on the same graph with regular measurements.
The real warning sign is a clear plateau in the child's own line.
Age at implantation is among the strongest factors; the plasticity of the brain's auditory pathways is highest in the first years.
Children with meaningful hearing experience through hearing aids before the implant usually progress faster.
How many hours a day the processor is worn directly determines how much sound input there is for learning.
Family involvement, a rich language environment and resources are also strongly linked to outcomes.
In children with additional developmental or neurological needs, progress may be slower, and goals are adapted accordingly.
Anatomical conditions such as an inner ear anomaly or a thin cochlear nerve also affect expectations.
In the first months after activation, the map is updated at frequent intervals.

cumleler.yazi: CAP, SIR and parent scales are repeated at regular intervals, for example every few months, especially in the first years.
cumleler.ses: C A P, S I R and parent scales are repeated at regular intervals, for example every few months, especially in the first years.

cumleler: Aided thresholds and speech perception are measured with age-appropriate behavioral tests.
Language and speech development is usually assessed once a year with age-appropriate standard tests.
At the move to preschool and school, classroom acoustics, remote microphones and informing the teacher come into focus.

maddeler.metin: s and sh confused: high-frequency access
Startles at loud sounds: comfort levels

cumleler: The therapist's notes are valuable for the audiologist; for example, constant confusion of s and sh suggests poor high-frequency access.
A child who startles at loud sounds or wants to remove the processor may need comfort levels reviewed.
If eye blinking or facial twitching is noticed during stimulation, it is reported to the audiologist right away.
A sudden loss of skills already gained is checked for a device fault or another problem.
The audiologist also tells the therapist about map changes, so information flows both ways within the team.

sahneler.metin: At every visit, plot CAP, SIR and data logging on the same graph. If you see a plateau, first check hours of use and the map, then additional needs.

cumleler.yazi: A clinical tip: at every visit, plot CAP, SIR and daily hours of use from data logging on the same follow-up graph.
cumleler.ses: A clinical tip: at every visit, plot C A P, S I R and daily hours of use from data logging on the same follow-up graph.

cumleler: This graph is also a powerful tool for showing progress to the family.
If you see a plateau in the line, first check hours of use and the map, then middle ear status.
If these are in order, discuss with the family a referral to specialists for additional developmental needs.

maddeler.metin: Activation is a start; the brain learns
Goal: a year per hearing year

cumleler: Implant activation is a beginning; the child learns step by step to make sense of sound, from awareness to understanding.
All-day processor use and family involvement in daily routines are the basis of progress.

cumleler.yazi: CAP tracks auditory performance, SIR speech intelligibility, and IT-MAIS listening behavior in infants.
cumleler.ses: C A P tracks auditory performance, S I R speech intelligibility, and I T mays listening behavior in infants.

cumleler: The general goal is one year of language growth per year of hearing; a plateau in the line calls for a team review.

sahneler.soru: What does category 7 mean on the CAP?
secenekler: Phone use with a familiar talker
sahneler.aciklama: CAP 7: using the phone _with a familiar talker_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in the Categories of Auditory Performance, or CAP, which skill does category 7 show?
cumleler.ses: Test yourself: in the Categories of Auditory Performance, or C A P, which skill does category 7 show?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: using the phone with a familiar talker.
This is the top category of the original scale; it requires understanding without seeing the speaker's face.
